auraIntro: Explorer, Whirlpool Galaxy is the textbook example of a grand design spiral galaxy, interacting with companion NGC 5195.
overview: The Whirlpool Galaxy (M51) is an iconic grand design spiral galaxy located approximately 31 million light-years away in the constellation Canes Venatici.
formation: Its distinct double spiral structure is driven by gravitational tidal encounters with smaller dwarf companion NGC 5195.
structure: A grand design spiral galaxy spanning 76,000 light-years, featuring sweeping spiral arms enriched with bright H II starbirth regions.
discoveryHistory: Discovered on October 13, 1773 by Charles Messier. Its spiral structure was first drawn in 1845 by Lord Rosse.
observationTips: A favorite for amateur astronomers; small telescopes reveal companion galaxy NGC 5195, while larger instruments show sweeping spiral arms.
funFacts: First celestial object ever identified as possessing a spiral structure (by Lord Rosse in 1845).
Tidal compression from companion galaxy NGC 5195 triggers massive waves of newborn star formation along its arms.

cards.title: Arrival: The Grand Design Archetype
cards.subtitle: Messier 51 Overview
cards.body: Welcome to the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51), the textbook archetype of a Grand Design spiral galaxy. Located 31 million light-years away according to NASA's Hubble catalog, M51 features clean, symmetric spiral arms stretching across 76,000 light-years, anchored by dwarf companion NGC 5195.

cards.title: Discovery: Unlocking Spiral Nature
cards.subtitle: From Charles Messier to Lord Rosse
cards.body: Discovered on October 13, 1773 by Charles Messier, M51 made history in 1845 when William Parsons (Lord Rosse) observed it using the 72-inch 'Leviathan of Parsonstown' telescope in Ireland. Lord Rosse's hand drawing of M51 was the first in history to capture a galaxy's spiral structure.
bulletPoints: Charles Messier cataloged M51 in 1773; Pierre Méchain found companion NGC 5195 in 1781.
Lord Rosse drew its spiral arms in 1845, coining the concept of 'spiral nebulae'.
Established spiral structures as a fundamental galactic morphology.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: Gravitational Tidal Engine
cards.subtitle: NGC 5195 Interaction & Starburst Waves
cards.body: M51's prominent spiral arms are sculptured by gravitational tidal interactions with companion galaxy NGC 5195. As NGC 5195 dipped behind M51 over 500 million years ago, its gravitational pull created density waves that compress gas, igniting thousands of bright blue young star clusters.
bulletPoints: Gravitational tides pump energy into M51's interstellar medium.
Density waves compress hydrogen gas to ignite widespread starbursts.
Bright pink H II regions trace active star nurseries along the arms.

visualPlaceholder.caption: Hubble Space Telescope close-up of tidal dust bridge connecting M51 to NGC 5195.

cards.title: Deep Insight: Webb Infrared Dust Filaments
cards.subtitle: MIRI & NIRCam Infrared Revelations
cards.body: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope imaged M51 with NIRCam and MIRI, revealing intricate networks of warm interstellar dust filaments that are totally dark in optical light. Webb traced organic molecules (PAHs) and warm dust lanes where new stars are forming inside dense dark clouds.
bulletPoints: JWST mid-infrared vision penetrates dark optical dust lanes.
Reveals glowing filamentary structures of warm silicates and complex molecules.
Maps embedded protostars hidden from visible light telescopes.

visualPlaceholder.title: JWST Infrared Scan of M51
visualPlaceholder.caption: JWST MIRI mid-infrared composite image revealing skeletal dust filaments in M51.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: Supernova Proving Ground
cards.subtitle: Stellar Deaths in M51
cards.body: M51's intense starburst activity creates many short-lived massive stars that end in catastrophic supernova explosions. In recent decades, astronomers have observed three major supernovae in M51 (SN 1994I, SN 2005cs, and SN 2011dh), making M51 an active laboratory for stellar evolution.
bulletPoints: Observed 3 major supernovae within a 17-year span (1994, 2005, 2011).
High star formation rate continuously yields massive stellar progenitor candidates.
SN 2011dh allowed direct pre-explosion identification of a yellow supergiant star.
